#4944. 12 Health Benefits of Pilates That Make It Worth the Hype, According to a Physical Therapist

Say hello to core strength, better endurance, and less back pain.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s a reason Pilates has a reputation of being a leg-shaking, muscle-quaking workout. But it’s more than just a hard workout—it ended up being a total game changer for my health.

As an orthopedic physical therapist and conditioning coach, I’ve built my life around strength, health, and movement. Sports have always been central to who I am—running, weightlifting, and higher-intensity training used to be my norm—though my body hasn’t always kept up.

Then, last summer, I took my first reformer Pilates class at Bodyrok, a 45-minute full-body group fitness class. It was humbling—I engaged muscles I rarely worked in traditional strength training sessions (hello, core) and tackled moves I had never done before. But slowing down and focusing on controlled movements also felt surprisingly satisfying.

After eight months of consistent reformer Pilates classes (plus running and strength training sessions), I finally understood the hype. It has strengthened my core and pelvic muscles, improved circulation to alleviate pain, and eased inflammation. Plus, it complements my sport performance because it targets stabilizer muscles and mobility.

Here’s why both mat and reformer Pilates truly deliver, according to research.

Of all the benefits Pilates offers, it’s most famous for its focus on core strength—a key foundation for nearly everything we do, from lifting a baby and swinging a golf club to simply maintaining good posture at a desk. More specifically, Pilates targets the deep stabilizing muscles of the core, including the often overlooked transverse abdominis, as well as the rectus abdominis, or your six-pack muscles.

Want to pair Pilates and strength training in a streamlined way? Try the Women’s Health+ Pilates x Lift workout plan, a four-week program that gives you the best of both modalities to build muscle, improve mobility, and protect your joints.

Pilates combines controlled movements that lengthen and stretch your muscles, helping improve flexibility and range of motion within a joint. In fact, just six weeks of Pilates may improve functional mobility, according to research in the Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies. By working your muscles through their full range of motion, Pilates makes everyday activities like climbing stairs and bending down to tie your shoes feel easier and more fluid.

Most of us spend hours hunched over computers, then move straight to our phones or the TV, which can wreak total havoc on our posture. Fortunately, Pilates can undo those habits by strengthening the core and upper back, stabilizing the shoulders, and opening up the chest.

Research supports these benefits: A 2024 systematic review published in Archives of Rehabilitation Research and Clinical Translation found that after eight weeks of Pilates, sedentary women showed improvements in both posture and their ability to perform daily activities. Pilates also emphasizes proper form and alignment, so you’re constantly practicing better posture during your workouts—a habit that, with practice, can naturally carry over into everyday life.

Pilates isn’t just about your core—it’s a full-body workout that fires up multiple muscle groups at once, building strength from head to toe, especially when using a reformer for added resistance. In fact, a 2025 randomized trial published in Nature found that women who practiced reformer Pilates for 60 minutes three times per week for eight weeks saw measurable gains in muscle mass, grip strength, and body composition.

Research also shows that Pilates can boost muscular endurance, or the ability of your muscles to perform repeated contractions or maintain a position against resistance over time.

What truly sets Pilates apart, though, is its focus on the smaller stabilizing muscles most people ignore, which play a key role in controlled, efficient movement. Because of this, Pilates can enhance functional movement patterns, making it a secret weapon for better performance and fewer injuries.

The functional strength and stability aspects of Pilates make it an excellent complement to heavy lifting (which you should still do two to three times a week to develop bone density, improve metabolic health, and develop muscular power). That’s because a strong core protects against injury (like lower back pain) and helps you maintain good form even when handling a heavy barbell, per 2023 research in Healthcare.

Pilates is all about syncing breath, focus, and fluid movement, encouraging a deep connection between the mind and body. Each exercise requires careful attention to form, encouraging intentional, controlled movement that can feel almost meditative. This mindfulness, combined with the focus on strengthening the mind-body connection (the two-way link between your mental state and physical health), naturally supports mental well-being.

Because breathing is central to Pilates, it can also reduce stress and promote a sense of calm. As a matter of fact, doing Pilates just once a week for an hour over the span of three months can improve anxiety, depression, and stress, according to 2025 research in Healthcare.

About 80 percent of adults in the U.S. will experience lower back pain at some point in their lives, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH). But Pilates can help relieve that pain, as it stabilizes the core and improves posture, according to a 2025 study in the Irish Journal of Medical Science. The study had 66 participants ages 18 to 65 with lower back pain either do Pilates three times a week or a home exercise program (involving stretching, strengthening, and mobility exercises) for eight weeks. The group that did Pilates experienced improvements in pain relief, functional disability, and quality of life, compared to those who did the home exercise program.

Additionally, a 2022 review in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy looked at 118 trials to find out the best exercise options for reducing pain and disability in adults with chronic lower back pain. It looked at aerobic, strength, combined aerobic and strength, core-based, McKenzie (movements designed to relieve musculoskeletal pain), Pilates, stretching, and mind-body exercise. It found that Pilates, core-based, and mind-body exercise were the best for reducing pain—but Pilates had the highest likelihood for lowering pain and disability.

Your balance decreases as you age, according to the NIH, but not if you do something about it. A 2021 study in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health observed the effects of Pilates training on balance and fall risk in older women. It had 50 women over 60 years old either do two Pilates sessions for three months, or no exercise outside of everyday activities. Before and after training, the women did exercises like the single-leg stance and Timed Up and Go (where you stand from a sitting position, walk, and then do it in reverse), and other tests. The group that did Pilates improved their balance and lowered their fall risk more than the group that didn’t exercise.

One 2021 review of literature on exercise and longevity in Aging shows how regular exercise can slow down cellular aging—and Pilates is a great fitness modality to support strength, mobility, and confidence as we age. Since it’s low-impact and lower intensity, it can help build strength without overstressing your joints, making it a sustainable workout for now and the future.

In fact, in a 2025 study in the Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies, 24 adults age 76, on average, either did 20 weeks of an online Pilates program or no exercise. Their balance, core stability, and functional fitness were tested with exercises like the single-leg stance, 6-minute walk test, and core muscle strength and stability tests. The study found that the Pilates program improved balance, cardiorespiratory endurance, and core strength in older adults, especially compared to the group that didn’t exercise.

Both mat and reformer Pilates can provide all of the benefits above, but they also have some of their own distinct draws. Reformer Pilates, specifically, can be really useful for training muscle patterns in a gentle way—by using springs for resistance rather than gravity, WH previously reported. (Think: footwork while lying down on a reformer rather than a standing squat with a barbell.) As a result, you’re able to relax more into each move, making it a lower-impact workout.

And with its moving carriage, the Pilates reformer can be a valuable tool for building greater balance and stability, as it creates a greater challenge than you’d get on solid ground with a mat workout.

What’s more, a reformer can help support someone rehabbing from an injury—particularly because it can help correct misaligned movement patterns more effectively than simply completing a bodyweight move.

Perhaps the best part of any Pilates modality? It’s for anyone and everyone, no matter your age or fitness level. While some Pilates classes (i.e., those using reformers) can be intimidating and costly, you actually don’t need any equipment to get started. Pilates can be done with just your body and a workout mat, and you can even replicate reformer-style moves using sliders, foam rollers, and towels.

No matter how you practice, the focus on controlled movement and mindful breathing makes Pilates a real game changer for athletic performance and holistic wellness. Trust me, I speak from experience.

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. She is a graduate of Emory University and Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism. Her work has appeared in Women's Health, POPSUGAR, Food & Wine, What To Expect, Cosmopolitan, Men's Health, and elsewhere. As a former collegiate pole vaulter, she loves all things fitness and has yet to meet a group workout class she doesn't like.

#4943. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: Is Worrying About Sleep Keeping Us Awake?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

As a busy, sleep-deprived, middle-aged father of two young kids, including an irrepressible 8 year old ball of energy who is, without fail, up and ready to take on the world at 6 o’clock every morning (usually with a steady stream of questions about dinosaurs, the natural world and the origins of the universe in his back pocket), do I really need another set of headlines informing me that not only am I falling short in getting the requisite 40 winks a night but I’m also at risk of 83 diseases into the bargain?

Another day, another headline-grabbing sleep study lands, this time linking a greater amount of sleep – specifically sleep of the rapid eye movement (REM) variety, also known as dream sleep – to a lower risk of dozens of diseases.

The recent study published in PLOS Medicine found that REM sleep is linked to a lower risk of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis (MS). As an added bonus, the study also found that a higher amount of deep sleep was associated with a lower risk of seven health conditions, including depression and type 2 diabetes.

So far, so alarming for a self-confessed “bad sleeper”.

Yet also fairly unsurprising. The accepted science, combined with anecdotal experience, has long told us that the right amount of good quality sleep corresponds directly with improved short and long-term health outcomes, both mental and physical. Evidence suggests that 7-9 hours of sleep per night is typically the sweet spot for a healthier life. Where this particular study differs from those that have come before is that scientists used wrist trackers to gather much more detailed information over a multi-year timeline about participants’ sleep stages, including irregular sleep patterns and variations in sleep duration. The findings were drawn from real-world data from more than 95,000 participants in the UK Biobank database.

Now, as the aforementioned and self-proclaimed VBP (very busy person – if you know, you know), who works long hours across UK and US timezones for the day job whilst serving as a sub-par encyclopedia for the real boss (the aforementioned 8 year old) outside of work, the general demands and pressures of daily life are more than sufficient to make consistently good sleep something that is all too often out of reach.

I know this to be true because the wearable I use reminds me of the fact with cold, hard data on a daily, if not hourly, basis. One of the first things my wife and I do each morning (after fending off existential questions from a third grader) is hawkishly plug into our Oura app to trade sleep scores and discuss what did or didn’t contribute to our invariably bad or, very rarely, good night’s sleep. Deep sleep, REM sleep, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, latency, even sleep debt – a laundry list of data points that we pore over in a futile attempt to make our sleep consistency optimal whilst living a life that doesn’t readily allow for it. Scientists have even given this phenomenon a name – Orthosomnia – where the anxiety of analyzing and perfecting sleep scores actually disrupts rest and intensifies poor sleep, and in the most extreme cases, insomnia.

It turns out we’re not alone. Results of a Gallup poll from 2024 – with the rather on-the-nose headline “Americans sleeping less, more stressed” – showed Americans report averaging 6.5 hours of sleep per night, comfortably below the recommended baseline of 7+ hours. Perhaps more tellingly, in a survey from 2024, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that nearly 70% of Americans report losing sleep due to anxiety.

Which brings me back to my original point. Anxiety-induced stress makes for the perfect bedfellow (pun intended) for a bad night’s sleep. The kind of anxiety-induced stress that can be both caused and amplified by obsessing over wearables data and a steady torrent of sleep-related content that aims to scaremonger rather than inform.

In fairness to the UK Biobank study, it is unequivocally important and unique research steeped in actionable real-world data and peer-reviewed medical science. And yet we live in a world increasingly awash with AI-generated content, sporting sensationalist headlines and powered by algorithms designed with an inherent imbalance to engage rather than empower. In that environment, gold-standard scientific work like this is all too often reduced to the lowest common denominator.

If you’ll indulge a minor tooting of our own horn here, this is precisely the inverse of how the team of wonderfully talented editorial misfits at Healthline Media thinks about and creates health information. We take research-backed science and our embedded clinical rigor and apply it to every aspect of our work. But we never lose sight of the fact that behind every study, there’s someone lying awake in the early hours running the math on their own risk factors, and that what they need in that moment is recognition that we are all at different stages on that journey, and a helping hand along the path to better health.

Life isn’t linear, sleep isn’t linear, and health is certainly not linear. Some nights I’ll get my seven hours. Plenty of others I won’t. And that is ok. Because either way, my alarm clock has a favorite dinosaur and a nonnegotiable 6 a.m. start time, and no peer-reviewed study or scary headline is going to change that. So I’ll take the data and the empathy, leave the anxiety, and see you all again at dawn.

If there’s something keeping you awake at night, or you just want to learn more about the wonderful world of sleep, we have a wealth of science-backed information at our dedicated Sleep Health hub. There you can also find Healthline’s Better Sleep Challenge – a three-week series designed to help you sleep better, feel more rested, and wake up ready to thrive each day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4940. What You Should Know About Exercising When Bone Density Is a Concern

Osteopenia or osteoporosis doesn’t have to sideline your workouts. Here’s what to do, how to modify, and when to back off.

You might have heard that being active is a good idea when you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, conditions marked by lower-than-normal bone density. But when you’re exercising specifically to improve bone health, some types of exercise may be more helpful than others. Before lacing up your sneakers, there are a few things to know.

“When patients ask me what they can do to preserve and protect their bone health, consistent weight bearing and resistance exercises are the first things I recommend,” says Nicole Leung, MD, director of the Osteoporosis and Bone Health Program at NYU Langone Health in New York City. “Bone is a living tissue, so it adapts to mechanical load through remodeling.”

When bone tissue is stressed via physical activity, your body responds by making more bone, helping strengthen the tissue. Exercise also lowers the activity of cells that dissolve and break down old bone. That combo helps preserve or even improve your bone mineral density, regardless of your health status. Exercise may slow or even prevent the progression of osteoporosis; if you have osteoporosis already, it can help you maintain the bone you have and reduce your risk for falls and fractures.

A bone-density diagnosis doesn’t mean you have to give up exercise—but your routine should reflect your fracture risk and health history. Here’s what Dr. Leung recommends for choosing activities, adapting your routine, and knowing when to check with your doctor before making major changes.

There are a few types of activities that make up a bone-friendly exercise plan, and it’s important to get the right amount of each. Here are the types of exercise to do regularly.

These are exercises where you’re on your feet and putting force on your muscles and bones as they work against gravity. Depending on factors like your age, fitness level, and bone mineral density, these activities can include:

People working to maintain their bone health should do these sorts of activities for 30 to 60 minutes, three to five days per week, according to the American College of Sports Medicine.

As for activities like swimming and cycling, they’re great for getting your heart pumping—but because they’re low-impact, they won’t do much for your bones. That said, feel free to do them in addition to your weight-bearing exercises if you enjoy them.

Lifting (relatively) heavy things works your muscles and helps build bone density. This includes free weights, machines, resistance bands, or body weight exercises like squats or push-ups. Aim for two to three strength sessions per week, and don’t be afraid to gradually go heavier (with your doctor’s okay). Pushing yourself to 70 to 90 percent of your max effort may deliver a bigger bone boost than lifting lighter weights, research suggests.

Having osteoporosis makes you more prone to fractures after falls, but you can strengthen your balance—and reduce your chances for a broken bone—with exercises like yoga, tai chi, or Pilates. “Any exercise where you have to shift your body weight side to side and forward and back can be very helpful for your stabilizing muscles,” Dr. Leung says. She recommends working balance exercises into your schedule a few times per week. Find safe modifications if you’re worried about falling, like holding onto a sturdy chair or touching a wall.

Whether you’ve been exercising for years, are just starting out, or are returning to a routine after a long hiatus, Dr. Leung advises paying attention to your posture, avoiding exercise when you’re overly exhausted, and increasing intensity gradually. Older women who are new to exercise can still do resistance training, she says, but may need to start at a slower pace and under supervision.

Despite the overall benefits of exercise, you still need to be careful, particularly when you have osteoporosis. Certain activities can set the stage for potential spine fractures, so before starting an exercise program, decide with your doctor or other qualified professional what is and isn’t safe for you.

According to the International Osteoporosis Foundation, you may need to limit or avoid moves that involve:

Yoga, while helpful for balance, can involve poses that put your spine at risk (like forward bends, deep twists, plow pose, shoulder stand, and pigeon pose). If you decide to give it a try, choose a class where the teacher can offer safe modifications, Dr. Leung says. It’s also best to steer clear of activities that come with a high risk of falling from above standing height, like skiing or horseback riding, she adds.

When it comes to stressing your bones, it’s possible to get too much of a good thing. “Overburdening your bone can actually lead to stress fractures,” Dr. Leung says. If you do prolonged intense weight-bearing and high-impact exercises like jogging or jumping rope, avoid scheduling them on back-to-back days. Alternate those workouts with activities like strength training, or have an active recovery day where you walk or do yoga or tai chi, she recommends.

Make it a point to stay active even after you’ve completed the day’s workout. According to Dr. Leung, non-exercise activities like casual walking or doing chores may help to maintain bone density when compared to sedentary behavior. Stroll over to chat with a coworker at their desk during a break, take the stairs when you can, or walk while you call a friend instead of sitting. A few minutes here and there can really add up.

Any new or worsening bone or spine pain is a warning sign to stop exercising and contact your doctor. You should also call your doctor if you fall while exercising, notice that you’ve had height loss, or if your spine appears curved, which could be signs of a spinal fracture. And always stop exercising and seek medical attention if you experience other severe symptoms like dizziness, faintness, or chest pain.

Consistency counts. People with low bone density who stay active over several months tend to see the greatest bone-health benefits, studies show. Choose activities you enjoy, build up gradually, and find a rhythm you can sustain. The goal isn’t to nail every workout—it’s to keep movement in your life.

#4939. When Your Cofounder Partnership No Longer Fits

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

For the cofounder who has outgrown the partnership, it feels tight. You notice yourself getting smaller in meetings. You wonder whether the partnership is worth it. Eventually you stop giving feedback, because what's the point, and the resentment piles up. People in this seat often leave.

A friend of mine lived a version of this. He was carrying most of his company's day-to-day operations when he walked away.

On the surface, the conflict with his two partners concerned go-to-market strategy, and they had debated it repeatedly without resolution. Underneath those debates was a shift in an agreement the three of them had never stated aloud.

When he joined the company, his partners were roughly 20 years his senior, considerably more experienced, and already financially successful. He was early in his career and still working toward his first million.

The terms of their arrangement were never written down, yet all three understood them. He would defer to their judgment, and their opinions would carry more weight. They would serve as his mentors, and he would turn their ideas into a functioning product.

His partners found meaning in the mentor role—giving back to a younger founder was gratifying for them. He received an education he could not have purchased, and in exchange he declined other opportunities and accepted reduced income while the company was not yet profitable. For the first few years, the arrangement held.

In Marital Tensions (1967), the psychiatrist Henry Dicks, drawing on his work with couples at London's Tavistock Clinic, described what he called unconscious working agreements: unspoken contracts shaped by how two partners' needs and defenses fit together. Neither partner designs such an agreement intentionally, yet both maintain it. Dicks termed this shared maintenance collusion, a word that refers to joint participation, largely outside of awareness.

Founders often describe the beginning of a partnership as chemistry. Some of that synergy reflects genuine liking for one another and complementary skill sets. Some of it reflects two sets of unconscious needs fitting together, and those needs change over time.

Two or three years in, my friend had internalized how his partners thought and began developing views of his own. He was also carrying a disproportionate share of the operational load, which tends to sharpen one's opinions quickly. He came to see their go-to-market thinking as outdated, and he said so.

The original agreement had no room for that. It had been built for a junior partner, and he no longer occupied that role.

This is the dynamic founders tend to underestimate. They revisit equity and titles as the company matures. But the unspoken agreement rarely receives the same attention, largely because no one remembers entering into it.

For the partners on the other side, the change can register as betrayal, as though someone were breaking terms that were never stated. What they are losing may be something they would never admit to needing, such as being looked up to. Between one partner's constriction and the other's sense of betrayal, an honest conversation becomes considerably harder to begin.

So why does a shift in power show up as a fight about a business-related issue? Because that topic is safe to talk about. Most partnerships run on operational language: targets, roadmaps, tasks. Talking about status and need requires a different vocabulary, and using it requires vulnerability.

For my friend, the honest version would have sounded something like this: I've learned a lot from you, I now disagree with you on some big things, and I need that to be okay. Saying that aloud carries genuine interpersonal risk, but creates the opportunity for the group to evolve.

Instead, he challenged their strategy. Because he never named the shift in power, his objections did not land, and eventually he left.

These deals are hard to see from the inside. One useful clue is a reaction that's out of proportion to the issue. You replay the meeting at night. You vent to your spouse, your friends, your coach. That intensity often means something under the surface is asking to be updated.

Therapists who practice acceptance and commitment therapy sometimes describe two climbers on separate mountains. From across the valley, I can spot the boulder on your trail more easily than you can, and you can spot mine. Cofounders are climbing the same mountain, which is part of why an outside view from a specialist helps.

Before you talk to your cofounder, it helps to get honest with yourself. Think back to when you started. What were you counting on them for? Energy, encouragement, being the one who knew more? And what did you quietly offer in return? Some of those terms probably still fit. Some were written for people you no longer are.

Then have one conversation, in plain language. You don't need clinical terms, and you don't need to be a therapist. Open by saying you'd like to talk about the recent disagreements and about how the partnership itself has changed, and that you want to hear their view too. Then speak for yourself: Say what has changed in you, and that you know it has created friction. Then ask what they've noticed.

From there, make one concrete change to how you decide things, such as who has the final call in which areas. Try it, then adjust. Write it down, and look at it again in a year. The original deal may never become fully conscious, and that's fine. What matters is that the partnership catches up to the people in it, so your next disagreement about the plan can actually be about the plan.

Dicks, H. V. (1967). Marital tensions: Clinical studies towards a psychological theory of interaction. Routledge & Kegan Paul.

#4938. FDA Issues Class II Blood Pressure Medication Recall, Over 13,000 Bottles Affected

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Some people taking a common blood pressure medication may have pills that don’t dissolve the way they should.More than 13,500 bottles of 25 mg chlorthalidone tablets are under a nationwide recall after failing lab tests, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).Inventia Healthcare Limited voluntarily recalled the tablets on September 3, 2026, according to the FDA’s enforcement report.

The report lists the reason for the recall as “Failed Dissolution Specifications.” That means the tablets failed a test that measures how the medicine is released from the pill, according to the FDA.“Chlorthalidone is a diuretic, or ‘water pill,’ commonly used to treat high blood pressure and reduce excess fluid retention in the body,” Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, told Healthline.This is the second time this year Inventia has recalled its 25 mg chlorthalidone tablets.

The first recall was initiated on June 5 and covered 11,460 bottles. Both were for the same reason: failed dissolution specifications, according to FDA enforcement reports.

Together, the June and September recalls cover 25,027 bottles.

The FDA classified both recalls as Class II.

The two recalls cover three batches of the chlorthalidone tablets, USP, 25 mg, according to the FDA enforcement reports. All three expire in April 2027.

The 25 mg tablets are light yellow, round and flat, with “103” stamped on one side and nothing on the other, according to the drug label.

Recall initiated on September 3, 2026; 13,567 bottles affected.

Recall initiated on June 5, 2026; 11,460 bottles affected.

Patients whose supply is part of the recall “should contact their pharmacy to discuss obtaining a replacement and ask whether they should continue taking the medication in the meantime,” Chen said.

For Class II recalls, people can generally keep taking the medicine unless the recalling company gives other instructions, according to the FDA.

In some cases, stopping a medication may be more harmful than continuing to take the recalled medicine, the agency said.

If you’re concerned that your medication has been recalled, here’s what you can do:

A Class II recall means using the drug may cause temporary health problems, but the chance of serious harm is unlikely, according to the FDA.

“The voluntary recalls cited are classified as Class II, at the retail level,” an FDA Spokesperson told Healthline.

A retail-level recall means the company is “removing the product from retail stores and pharmacy shelves,” Ileana Elder, a branch chief in the FDA’s Office of Compliance, said in an FDA podcast. When a recall doesn’t extend to consumers, stopping a medication unnecessarily can be more harmful, and patients should contact their pharmacy with questions, Elder said.Healthline reached out to the companies for more information about the September recall, but had not heard back by the time of publication. The FDA referred further questions to the companies

However, based on a preliminary assessment of the batches recalled in June, Rising Pharma Holdings, a distributor of one of the recalled lots, stated that “no impact on patient health and safety is anticipated.”

“If a medication does not dissolve at the expected rate, it may not be absorbed by the body as intended,” Chen said. “This can reduce the amount of medication that reaches the bloodstream and potentially decrease its effectiveness.”

In a dissolution test, a lab places a tablet in a controlled liquid medium to determine whether and how quickly the active ingredient is released, according to FDA guidance on dissolution testing.

A failed result means the batch didn’t meet the release standard set for that product, according to FDA guidance on drug quality standards.Manufacturers propose and justify these standards, and regulators approve them as part of drug approval, according to the same guidance.

In the United States, the official standards stay the same from the time a drug is released until it expires, the guidance said.The September FDA enforcement report doesn’t say how the recalled tablets failed. A notice from Rising Pharma Holdings about the June recall provides more details.

Rising found two problems at the 18-month mark of ongoing quality testing of its 25 mg tablets, the company said in a notice posted by the California State Board of Pharmacy:

According to the drug label, chlorthalidone treats:

The label recommends that most people with high blood pressure start with one 25 mg dose per day. That’s the strength involved in both 2026 recalls.

#4936. Erin and Sara Foster Reveal the Rule That Keeps Their Business—and Sisterhood—Working

The Nobody Wants This producers stop by the latest episode of The Huddle.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’ve binged all three seasons of the Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, presided over a board meeting in your chicest Favorite Daughter blazer, or nodded along to a cringey dating anecdote while listening to The World’s First Podcast, you are no doubt familiar with the work of multi-hyphenate sisters Erin and Sara Foster.

Raised in Los Angeles (dad is famous record producer David Foster), the sisters first gained notoriety with their VH1 mockumentary series, Barely Famous, in 2015. Since then, they’ve gone on to launch several successful businesses, including their clothing line and a production company, Fatigue Sisters Productions. (They even recently served as guest sharks on ABC’s Shark Tank.)

With the season 3 premiere of Nobody Wants This (based on Erin’s own experience of dating and marrying a Jewish man and later converting to Judaism), the dynamic duo stopped by the Women’s Health podcast The Huddle to chat with editors Abby Cuffey and Jacqueline Andriakos about doing business together, setting boundaries, and raising kids.

Erin and Sara launched their clothing line, Favorite Daughter, in late 2020 to fill gaps in their own closets. But as the company has grown and evolved over time, they’ve learned to put their customers at the heart of everything they do. It’s also forced the sisters to staff up with people who are willing to share their true opinions, rather than simply being yes-men or yes-women.

“That's something that is really challenging when you have a talent-focused brand,” Erin says. “It's taken a very long time for us to convince the people who work for us to be honest with us. That’s how people become monsters—no one's telling them the truth.”

“I always say, too, this is a democracy,” Sara adds. “This only works if everyone feels heard. This only works if you're allowed to do the thing that you're hired to do.”

Having a valued third or even fourth opinion also comes in handy when the two can’t see eye-to-eye, which happened often when the brand first launched.

“We’re in a good place today, but we would have blow-up screaming fights in fittings for many years at Favorite Daughter,” Erin says. “It’s tricky for us, because we do not have differentiated, carved-out roles. We have the exact same role, so if we disagree, it's really challenging to find the happy medium.”

In 2021, the sisters’ working relationship expanded further when they launched their podcast The World's First Podcast with Erin & Sara Foster. While the duo aren’t shy about diving into personal topics—be it romantic relationships or raising children—they have set certain boundaries to ensure their friends and family don’t end up embarrassed or as headline fodder.

“I have an idea of where [my husband’s] boundaries are,” Erin says. “He's not really into me talking about exes or other relationships.”

Sara, on the other hand, learned the hard way where one of her daughter’s boundaries lie when she revealed her juvenile arthritis diagnosis—in the hopes of helping other parents—and it was picked up by multiple outlets.

“It never occurred to me that that could happen,” Sara says. “My daughter was like, ‘I do not appreciate that.’ I was like, ‘Oh god, I'm so sorry.’”

Given that they have creative control over the podcast’s content, Erin and Sara do occasionally edit out portions that they think could be taken out of context with the TikTok-ification of media nowadays. “We try to err on the side of keeping things in, but then there's some times that you get a little ahead of yourself,” Erin says.

Speaking of raising daughters, Sara’s got even more wisdom to share on parenting—specifically about telling your kids the harsh truths about yourself.

“Being a mother is just such a exercise in getting humbled,” she says. “My instinct was always like, don't reveal yourself too much. Don't let them see your flaws. Don't tell them about all the times you f---ed up as a teenager yourself. But that's the opposite. You're really supposed to. Maybe some people disagree with this, but as they get older, you’re supposed to reveal mistakes you made, things that you wish you did differently... That has changed the dynamic with me and my older daughter—being honest with her about things that I wish I had done differently.”

Erin agrees: “I think it's probably better for your children to grow up knowing that you are a complicated, flawed person, and then you don't have to fall off a pedestal for them.”

To hear more from the sisters about how they find the creativity to create, their stance on kids and social media, and why they’re obsessed with a certain protein powder, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above!

#4935. Understanding Commitment Uncertainty in Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 14, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Commitment uncertainty is one of the major challenges couples may present with in couples therapy. Commitment is typically a fundamental part of an exclusive romantic relationship. It influences how partners invest in the relationship, identify with one another, and engage with their shared life. Yet, partners may become unsure whether they want to remain committed, whether the relationship will continue, or whether they want to keep investing in it. This is referred to as commitment uncertainty. Understanding this uncertainty is important because a lack of commitment is strongly associated with separation and divorce.

Commitment uncertainty emerges after partners have formed a mutually agreed-upon relationship, such as an exclusive monogamous relationship, and it differs from the uncertainty that can occur during early dating, when the relationship status has not yet been defined.

Several theoretical models describe two broad aspects of commitment. The first concerns wanting to be in the relationship, while the second concerns forces that encourage a person to remain in the relationship.

Research distinguishes these as dedication commitment and constraint commitment. Dedication includes a strong sense of couple identity, a desire for the relationship to continue long term, giving the relationship priority, and a willingness to sacrifice for it. As partners experience their relationship as meaningful and meeting their needs, they tend to pay less attention to alternatives. Constraint commitment refers to difficulties that bind partners together. These can include investments in the relationship, concerns about the well-being of a partner or children, financial circumstances, and social pressure. Constraints can encourage partners to remain together and may also encourage them to work on their relationship. However, constraint commitment alone is unlikely to be sufficient for a functional and healthy relationship in the long term.

Supported by research findings, my experience as a licensed psychologist counselling individuals and couples from all over the world revealed several ways in which commitment uncertainty can emerge in an intimate relationship.

Uncertainty may begin with an event that becomes a

turning point in the relationship. Such an event can lead partners to reevaluate their relationship and its future.

Commitment uncertainty may also develop slowly as connection and engagement between partners deteriorate. At the same time, partners may avoid confronting their uncertainty. Existing constraints, such as living together or having children, can help sustain the relationship and make it possible for partners to resist the growing uncertainty.

In other cases, commitment uncertainty may become apparent without a specific event. Partners may recognise fundamental compatibility problems and realise that critical issues in the relationship were not adequately considered earlier.

For some couples, uncertainty may have been present from the beginning of the relationship. A relationship may begin with low levels of adjustment and remain consistently low in adjustment.

Furthermore, there is a critical factor associated with commitment uncertainty: attachment insecurity, comprised of two dimensions, attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance. Relationship uncertainty is known to mediate the association between both attachment dimensions and commitment.

However, the two attachment dimensions are associated with uncertainty in different ways.

Attachment anxiety involves a strong desire for intimacy and protection alongside concerns about a partner's availability and commitment, fear of abandonment, and concerns about one's own value to the partner. Increasing attachment anxiety is also associated with jealousy and greater emotional ups and downs.

Attachment avoidance, on the other hand, involves discomfort with closeness and dependence, less reliance on relationship partners for care, and a preference for distance. Lower trust in partners and perceptions of others as negative or unreliable are seen as factors associated with increased doubts about the relationship.

The indirect association with commitments was stronger for attachment anxiety than for attachment avoidance.

Both external and internal factors can contribute to the persistence of commitment uncertainty.

External constraints can make it difficult to act on uncertainty. Concern about children, for example, may encourage partners to remain together and attempt to work through their difficulties. Financial constraints may have a similar effect. These pressures can help couples remain together while facing uncertainty, but they can also result in partners staying together without addressing the underlying uncertainty, potentially contributing to increasing negativity in the long term.

Internal processes can also interfere with fully addressing uncertainty. Denial, dissociation, and avoidance may reduce contact with the emotional turmoil associated with uncertainty. Such processes may also be expressed behaviourally, including through an affair.

First of all, commitment uncertainty can concern either a person’s own commitment to the relationship or their perception of their partner’s commitment.

Secondly, it is useful to consider dedication and constraint commitment, as these different aspects can help clarify the nature of the couple's commitment and how it developed.

For example, a feeling of having been trapped by circumstances may indicate that commitment was not fully established initially and may contribute to continuing uncertainty.

During a course of my integrative couples therapy, online or in person, I tend to discuss commitment uncertainty during joint sessions and explore it further in individual sessions, while establishing clear boundaries and explicit confidentiality arrangements from the outset.

A particularly difficult situation arises when couples describe their position as: “I would be more committed if things improved.” The “things” may include communication, intimacy, or other difficulties within the relationship.

This creates a “chicken-and-egg” dilemma. A partner may say that commitment will follow improvement, while the lack of commitment itself reduces motivation to change relationship behaviour.

There may be two possible ways of addressing this dilemma. The couple may directly address whether the relationship should continue, or they may temporarily put the question of commitment aside and work on other relationship difficulties.

Some couples may agree to set aside questions about continuing the relationship for a set period. This can provide stability while they work on the relationship and prevent the possibility of separation from becoming a bargaining tool during everyday disagreements.

If the purpose of couples therapy is instead to clarify the future of the relationship, commitment itself needs to remain central to the work. The process involves examining the factors influencing the decision, considering the consequences of staying or leaving, and distinguishing relationship distress from a desire to end the relationship.

Traditional measures of successful couples therapy often focus on improved relationship functioning or avoiding separation or divorce. However, for couples experiencing commitment uncertainty, remaining together is not necessarily the only possible outcome of therapy. The outcome may include separating well or achieving satisfactory individual well-being.

I find it important to focus couples therapy on reducing avoidance and increasing positive engagement with the question of commitment.

In addition, couples therapy should not rush towards a decision. A demand for certainty may itself represent avoidance; thus, space for thoughtful decision-making needs to be allowed.

To sum up, for couples experiencing commitment uncertainty, therapy may involve exploring how that uncertainty developed, what maintains it, and what they want the outcome of therapy to be.

Şenkal Ertürk, İ., Akyüz, A. N., & Büyükşahin Sunal, A. (2025). Attachment Insecurities and Commitment: The Mediator Role of Relationship Uncertainty. Psychological reports, 332941251351244. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/00332941251351244

Owen, J., Rhoades, G., Shuck, B., Fincham, F. D., Stanley, S., Markman, H., & Knopp, K. (2014). Commitment uncertainty: A theoretical overview. Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 3(4), 207–219. https://doi.org/10.1037/cfp0000028

#4932. Cutting Back on Ultra-Processed Foods May Help Ease Depression Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emerging research has linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) with an increased risk of depression. Now, a small study published September 23 in JAMA Psychiatrysuggests that reducing UPF intake may help ease depression symptoms.

There is no universally accepted definition of UPFs. However, a widely used classification system known as NOVA defines them as industrial formulations made primarily from substances extracted or derived from foods, often with additives not typically used in home cooking. Examples include soft drinks, packaged snacks, candy, sausages, hot dogs, and pastries.

Previous research has linked UPFs to an increased risk of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and other mental health conditions. In the new study, participants reduced their UPF intake by more than 85% and had significantly lower depression scores across three standard measures while following the low-UPF diet.

This small study included 20 participants who:

The participants also had to agree not to change medications, therapy, exercise, or sleep during the study.

Of the 20 participants enrolled in the study, 19 completed it. The average age was 44. Participants followed both their usual diet and a low-UPF diet during separate phases of the study, with the order randomly assigned.

Participants generally found the low-UPF diet acceptable and manageable. They also had lower depression and anxiety scores during the low-UPF diet phase compared with their usual diet.

On one commonly used depression measure, the PHQ-9, average scores declined from 8.68 during the usual diet phase to 5.53 during the low-UPF phase.

The study had several limitations, including its small sample size, reliance on self-reported dietary data, and uncertainty about which aspects of reducing UPFs may have contributed to the changes in symptoms.

The researchers also said that larger studies are needed to determine whether reducing UPF intake can improve depression symptoms.

Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study, agreed, noting that more research is needed to understand whether reducing UPFs directly improves depression symptoms or whether other aspects of the overall diet may be contributing to the observed benefit.

Dara Houp, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist with Pathways Psychological Services in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it’s important to distinguish ultra-processed foods from processed foods more broadly.

Routhenstein agreed that the distinction is important. “Processing is not inherently negative. Many nutritious foods are processed in some way.”

“I would not encourage people to simply label a food as ‘processed’ or ‘unprocessed’ and make decisions based on that label alone. I prefer to look at the overall dietary pattern, the nutritional value of the food, and what role that food plays in the diet. A packaged food can still provide meaningful nutrients and be part of an overall nutritious eating pattern,” she said.

There are various proposed mechanisms for how UPFs may affect mood.

For example, UPFs are often low in fiber, vitamins, and minerals, which can play important roles in brain health.

Houp noted that some ingredients found in UPFs, including artificial sweeteners such as aspartame, may affect the gut microbiome.

“Our gut is a primary location for producing neurotransmitters, responsible for manufacturing the vast majority – upward of 90% – of our body’s serotonin. When the gut microbiome is disrupted, it directly interferes with healthy neurotransmitter production,” she said.

Houp added that diets high in UPFs may be lower in antioxidant-rich foods, such as fruits and vegetables, which could contribute to oxidative stress. Research suggests that people with depression may have lower antioxidant levels and higher markers of oxidative damage.

Routhenstein also noted that researchers are investigating how UPF consumption may influence inflammation, metabolic health, and the gut-brain axis, all of which may have implications for mood.

Reducing your UPF intake can start with small, sustainable changes.

Routhenstein suggested starting by looking at the foods you eat most often rather than trying to overhaul your kitchen.

“Identify one or two foods that are frequent sources of UPFs and consider what you could realistically replace them with. For example, you might swap a daily sugary drink for water or sparkling water, or choose fruit, nuts, yogurt, or another minimally processed option in place of a packaged snack,” she said.

Other ways you can help reduce UPFs include:

Routhenstein added that you don’t have to eliminate convenience from your diet. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, canned fish, oats, plain yogurt, tofu, and other minimally processed foods can make healthy eating much more practical.

“The goal is not to eat a perfectly unprocessed diet. It is to gradually shift the overall pattern toward more nutrient-dense foods that provide fiber, protein, healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals,” she said.

#4930. What “The Invite” Reveals About Sexless Marriages

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

There’s a moment in The Invite, the 2026 dramedy by Olivia Wilde, that you could easily miss. It’s buried in the pre-orgy hilarity of the plot, which is intentional; humor is often used to camouflage our discomfort with sex. Pina, the vivacious and astute sexologist played by Penelope Cruz, asks the couple played by Wilde snd Seth Rogen, with the sincere curiosity of a scientist, “How do you have sex with each other? You are so mean to each other.”

Under the facade, lies the honest, uncomfortable truth.

As a sexologist, I’ve sat with countless people stuck in this intimacy no-man’s-land and it truly is a heartbreaking place. Sexless marriages are particularly hard to navigate because it is a deeply lonely place. Being in one is a hard thing to share, because it reeks of rejection. “My partner no longer desires me” is not something you can bring even to your closest confidante.

Sexless marriages are highly personal and therefore, difficult to define. There is a commonly applied standard of “less than 10 times a year," but who gets to decide? What makes a relationship "sexless" anyway?

Like many things in the world of sex and relationships, there is art and there is science to it. But the reality of sexless marriages is this: You decide if you’re in one. Typically, a sexless marriage is anchored less in how much sex you’re having and more in the desire discrepancy: You’re not having as much sex as you want.

Sexless marriages can be devastating to a relationship, fueling a build-up of guilt, dejection and resentment. And the longer it goes on, the wider the gap can be, making a sexless marriage a tough place for a relationship to end up in and an even tougher one to climb out of.

Studies show that it’s typically men who want more sex in a marriage. Is this biologically or culturally driven, because women have been taught to be frugal with their sexual impulse? Through my years exploring this topic, I’ve heard from many women who said they were the ones who wanted more sex—and that they were shamed for it. The pain of sexless marriages is real, and it cuts in both directions.

Culture matters too, especially the role of women in society — though its impact on sex in marriage isn’t intuitive. In traditional, patriarchal cultures, women are taught that their sexual role is to please their husbands and to produce children. In societies where women are more empowered, they exercise their right to say "no". So it may look like there are fewer sexless marriages in more traditional cultures, but that may be a function of convention, not choice.

Time impacts intimacy in marriage, too. Research shows that sexual satisfaction in newlyweds typically declines after 4-5 years. Life gets in the way — jobs, kids, and the like (although there is science that shows how to keep the spark going). Poor physical health and aging can be predictors of sexless marriages as well.

The Gottman Institute identified the four horsemen of a decaying relationship: criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling. Pina put it in simpler terms: You’re too mean to have sex.

Relationship expert Esther Perel has said, “Sexuality is a coded language for our deepest emotional needs, our wounds, our fears, our aspirations, our longings.” If a relationship doesn’t create an environment of safety, trust, and respect, true sexual intimacy will not sustain.

Make-up sex is glamorized. Sure, occasionally, sex is a great way to break through the tension of a fight, but what happens in the bedroom is a reflection of what happens outside it.

When I coach people in sexless marriages, there are five things I ask them to think about:

The Invite highlights the harsh truth that we will do anything to hide, escape, or deflect from the discomfort of rejection. But when it comes to sexless marriages, ownership and accountability are key, as is knowing that relationships morph over time and need its participants to evolve with it.

Every couple in a sexless marriage is quietly issuing this invitation to one other, whether they know it or not: Come back to care first. The rest will follow.

#4928. How to Lose Fat and Build Muscle Sustainably as a Busy Mom—Your Realistic 4-Step Plan

A strength coach for moms outlines the key strength training and diet habits to adopt for lasting change.

For many moms returning to exercise after pregnancy, losing fat while building muscle can feel like a daunting goal.

“The odds are good that you lost some muscle mass during pregnancy. Maybe you weren’t training as much as you normally did or you weren’t training at all,” says Bailey, coach and founder of Well Mamas Coaching, in a recent YouTube video.

However, body recomposition is a gradual process, she explains, and consistency—“sticking with it”—matters far more than getting everything right.

“It's not [about] doing it perfectly. It's not having an hour to yourself every single day to do all this magical meal prep and green juicing,” she says.

“It's just jumping back in when you can and not buying into the start-stop cycle of...start[ing] over on Monday and find[ing] a new plan.”

Strength training with progressive overload is a “gold standard” pillar of a realistic body recomposition plan, Bailey says.

Progressive overload means gradually making your workouts more challenging over time by increasing the weight, number of repetitions, or training frequency, or by reducing your rest periods.

“This type of strength training is what signals your body...to adapt, change, and rebuild the muscle fibers that we're tearing down during these workouts, which is what helps you build muscle,” Bailey explains.

She recommends focusing on compound exercises such as squats, lunges, deadlifts, hip thrusts, and the bench press because “you're recruiting multiple muscle groups.”

As for your workout schedule, she reassures viewers that you don't need to train “six times a week...for 45 to 60 minutes.”

“Four workouts a week, 30 minutes or less, with progressive overload and compound moves...is plenty,” she says.

By now, it's well established that muscle growth and repair depend on eating enough protein.

“If you're not eating enough protein to repair the tears that you create in your muscles when you work out, then your body doesn't have the amino acids it needs to build those muscle fibers,” Bailey says.

She recommends aiming for around 30g of protein per meal. That's broadly in line with research showing that consuming around 25-30g of protein per meal is associated with greater lean mass and both upper- and lower-body strength in healthy women.

Good options include lean meat, beans, and legumes, yogurt, cottage cheese, and canned tuna.

“Mild” is the key word, Bailey emphasizes.

A calorie deficit means consuming fewer calories than your body burns each day.

“Of course, you do need to be in some sort of caloric deficit in order for fat loss to occur,” she reminds viewers.

However, the size of that deficit matters.

She recommends a moderate deficit of around 200-400 calories below your maintenance intake.

“That's just enough to prompt your body to use stored fat for energy,” she explains. “However, it's not so much that your body starts cannibalizing muscle.”

Research supports the importance of avoiding an overly aggressive calorie deficit, with one study finding that eating more than 500 fewer calories than required impaired gains in lean mass.

She adds one caveat for breastfeeding moms.

“You want to go above what I would calculate if you weren't nursing—anywhere from 400-800 additional calories per day,” she says.

Bailey acknowledges this can be difficult for moms.

“Often sleep and stress feel like they're not within our control,” she says.

However, sleep is essential because it's during recovery that muscle adapts and grows.

“The muscle...broken down through resistance training...is rebuilt...during sleep, while we're recovering,” she explains.

She also references research showing that sleep duration influences body recomposition, with shorter sleep associated with less fat loss.

If “a solid eight hours” isn't realistic, she suggests finding even a few extra minutes by cutting back on doomscrolling or late-night TV.

She also notes that chronically elevated cortisol levels associated with stress may interfere with muscle-building processes, recommending outdoor walks, deep breathing, or even guided meditation in the shower to create small moments of calm.

Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

#4926. Can the BPC-157 ‘Wolverine’ Peptide Really Help With Pain and Recovery?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wellness seekers are increasingly turning to BPC-157, the wildly popular “Wolverine” peptide for injury recovery and pain relief, despite scant human evidence.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted in July to ease restrictions on it and several other peptides, recommending the injectable substances be made eligible for pharmacy compounding.

But before restrictions were eased, preliminary research suggests a rise in the use of the Wolverine peptide in recent years.

A September 2026 preprint analyzed more than 15 million medical records and identified 1,039 people with documented BPC-157 use.

The researchers found a roughly 33-fold increase in new users between 2020 and 2026.

The results, which were based on clinical records, have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

“The study found that BPC-157 use is largely hidden in clinical narrative rather than conventional prescription data,” said lead study author Venky Soundararajan, PhD, co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of nference.

“The proportion of newly documented BPC-157 users who were male rose from 57% in 2020 to 70% in 2026, a statistically significant trend,” he told Healthline.

“The user population for BPC-157 peptide is increasingly male in proportion and increasingly younger with each passing year.”

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide marketed and sold online for wellness.

Health claims about it and other peptides have spread on social media and in fitness circles and wellness communities, with high-profile advocates like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. touting their benefits.

Proponents of BPC-157 claim the injectable peptide promotes injury recovery, pain relief, and tissue healing. Some advocates claim that “stacking” the Wolverine peptide, particularly with TB-500, may enhance its effects.

The “Wolverine” peptide got its nickname from claims that it facilitates rapid healing, echoing the regenerative abilities of the fictional X-Men character of the same name.

This promise of pain relief and recovery may be what gives the Wolverine peptide its appeal.

Soundararajan’s study found that nearly 33% of patients reported using BPC-157 for pain relief. By comparison, just 4% of patients reported using BPC-157 for performance enhancement.

Across the cohort of 1,039 patients, 27% reported improvements.

“Pain relief was the dominant reported benefit, documented in 183 patients,” Soundarajan said. “Wound or tissue healing was reported in 38 patients and functional return in 34 patients.”

“Part of BPC-157’s appeal appears to be to patients who remain symptomatic after chronic, complex or previously treated musculoskeletal problems, signaling a clear clinical unmet need,” he said.

Bert Mandelbaum, MD, a sports medicine specialist, orthopedic surgeon, and co-director of the Regenerative Orthobiologic Center at Cedars-Sinai Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, said that everyone experiences pain, but warned about the risks of using the Wolverine peptide to treat it.

“There is zero indication that BPC-157 has any efficacy for pain,” he told Healthline. “There’s zero evidence that shows that it’s good for clinical healing, and we don’t really understand the safety profile of it.”

Human evidence of the possible benefits and safety of the Wolverine peptide is limited.

A 2025 systematic review of current BPC-157 literature found that it was dominated by preclinical research and low-grade human evidence. The review authors said there was insufficient clinical safety data to determine the peptide’s risks.

A small 2021 retrospective study on the effects of injectable BPC-157 on knee pain suggests the peptide could help repair tissue and regrow cartilage. However, the study followed just 16 participants, lacked a control group, and did not assess impacts on function or quality of life.

An even smaller 2025 intravenous safety pilot on BPC-157 use involved 2 participants. While no adverse effects were reported during the short study, the researchers acknowledged that larger studies are needed to confirm safety.

The July 23–24 FDA advisory vote added BPC-157 to the Section 503A bulk drug substances list, allowing pharmacies to include it in compounded medications.

The FDA’s 8-6 vote, with one abstention, greenlit BPC-157 in both free-base and acetate forms.

The recommendation did not make BPC-157 an FDA-approved drug, nor is it a component of an approved product. The federal health agency has yet to make final regulatory decisions on peptides.

“RFK Jr. policies are hurting Americans,” Mandelbaum said.

“This decision is ridiculous. It’s another step in the wrong direction. There’s no basis for any of this stuff.”

The safety profile of the Wolverine peptide for use in humans is largely unknown.

As such, BPC-157 is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency as an unapproved substance for athletes both in and out of competition.

The FDA notes that peptides like BPC-157 (free base) may be sensitive to product formulation, processing, environmental conditions, and impurities, which could degrade the products and reduce their effectiveness.

The health agency adds that it currently has limited safety information for how peptides like BPC-157 are administered.

Soundararajan explained that his study was unable to estimate the incidence or overall safety of BPC-157 because adverse events were captured retrospectively from routine clinical notes and are likely underreported.

“That said, the medical records examined contain both positive and negative patient experiences,” he said.

“Mood, sleep, skin, injection-site, and gastrointestinal symptoms are concrete safety outcomes among the few examined patient records with available evidence that deserve prospective measurement and discussions by healthcare providers with their patients who report using BPC-157.”

Some experts warn of short-term risks like infection at the injection site, but the long-term effects are not known.

“We don’t have publications of infections yet, but there are anecdotes of this,” Mandelbaum said.

“People are injecting their joints with this stuff, and you have no idea what it is. It’s not standardized. It’s not being regulated by the FDA, and I think people should recognize that. And although we haven’t proven it’s a safety hazard, we know it has no efficacy. So why do it? Why waste your money?”

Experts urge anyone considering BPC-157 or another peptide treatment to discuss it with their doctor first.

You might ask for evidence supporting its use, information on its quality, and whether there are alternatives with established safety and effectiveness profiles.

Mandelbaum noted there are many scientifically proven and safe alternatives to consider.

“We have spent the last 20 years developing an arsenal of biologics from PRP to bone marrow aspirate to adipose tissue to understanding glucosamine and hyaluronic acid,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job at studying these things. We’re getting to the point where we are understanding the complexities of biologics. It’s exciting, and it’s impactful.”

Mandelbaum vehemently opposed the use of unapproved peptides like BPC-157.

He likened its rise in popularity to a “Ponzi scheme” promoted by “gym rats” and “internet influencers” who “leverage and exploit the gap between hope and knowledge.” Just because the FDA eased restrictions, he said, doesn’t make them any safer or more legitimate.

That said, any use of unapproved peptides should also be disclosed to a doctor.

“A short, open and empathetic clinical conversation can turn invisible consumer use of products like BPC-157 into useful clinical information that can critically help inform current and future care for such patients that ensure the best possible outcomes,” Soundararajan said.

BPC-157 should not be combined with other experimental peptides until research determines the potential for adverse reactions or events. Long-term use of BPC-157 and other peptides marketed for wellness is not advised.

#4925. Why Some Partners Don't View Unfaithful Behavior as Cheating

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Trust remains one of the most significant hallmarks of successful relationships. So, when it comes to defining infidelity, do you know it when you see it? Apparently, different types of personalities view cheating differently. Research explains.

Gayle Brewer et al. (2023) examined different perceptions of infidelity in a piece aptly entitled “But It Wasn’t Really Cheating,” specifically examining the viewpoints and behaviors of individuals with Dark Triad traits.[i] They begin by recognizing the three Dark Triad traits as distinct but interrelated, sharing features of lack of empathy and self-centeredness. Within romantic relationships, they note that Dark Triad individuals prefer uncommitted, short-term pairings.

Regarding the distinctions between the categories, Brewer et al. define Machiavellianism as “a strategic, long-term approach to personal relationships,” endorsing manipulation and a willingness to exploit others, and narcissism as involving a sense of superiority and entitlement. Regarding psychopathy, they recognize its link with callousness and impulsiveness but distinguish between primary psychopathy (callousness) and secondary psychopathy (risk-taking and impulsivity). They also found that different dark personalities view infidelity differently.

Brewer et al. recognized five categories of infidelity: online, fantasized, emotional, sexual, and hidden attachment. They found that the Dark Triad traits of Machiavellianism and primary psychopathy predicted how distinct acts were perceived as infidelity, controlling for personal experience and demographic factors. And they explained why.

Brewer et al. explain that people who score high on Machiavellianism were not only less likely to view fantasizing as infidelity, but also less concerned with fantasy if it does not hinder their strategic objectives, such as to obtain status or control. Regarding the decreased likelihood of viewing expressed emotion as infidelity, they note that Machiavellianism is associated with attachment avoidance, preferring emotional and psychological independence, and discomfort with intimacy. Having a partner who has become emotionally attached to others may decrease the pressure they personally feel to exhibit intimacy and emotional closeness, resulting in feeling less distressed by their partner’s behavior.

Regarding the finding that people high in primary psychopathy were more apt to view emotional expression and fantasy as infidelity, Brewer et al. note that primary psychopathy is linked with a higher level of emotional jealousy. Therefore, they note, this link may reflect a higher amount of infidelity sensitivity. They also note that primary psychopathy is associated with less empathy and perspective taking, which could make it hard for someone with these characteristics to understand a partner's motivation for engaging in certain behavior. They give the examples of someone using sexual fantasy to achieve sexual release or having emotional relationships with others for companionship, noting that people high in primary psychopathy would be unable to separate these behaviors from others that present a more direct threat to the relationship.

Brewer et al. also found that individuals high in primary psychopathy were less likely to characterize sexual acts or hidden attachment as infidelity, perhaps reflecting a higher proclivity to engage in sexual infidelity themselves, facilitating justification of their own behavior. Brewer et al. also note that primary psychopathy is linked with self-serving sexual deception, making sexual infidelity and hidden attachment seem more acceptable or desirable.

Couples seeking relational quality and permanence should agree on what types of behaviors constitute infidelity and avoid activities that involve extra-relational temptation. Fulfilling relationships are characterized by trust, truth and transparency rather than deception. Plan accordingly, and date responsibly.

[i] Brewer, Gayle, Alexandra Guothova, and Dimitris Tsivilis. “‘But It Wasn’t Really Cheating’: Dark Triad Traits and Perceptions of Infidelity.” Personality and Individual Differences 202 (February 2023): 1–5.
